# Behavioral Design Specification: TL Error and Integrity Error Sequence Library

## 1. Scope

This specification describes the behavior of a verification sequence library used to generate and check TileLink-UL (TL-UL) error and integrity-error scenarios in a Comportable IP (CIP) UVM environment. The module is not a hardware RTL block; it provides reusable stimulus and checking behaviors.

The module must:

- Generate TL-UL transactions that are intentionally invalid, malformed, or integrity-corrupted.
- Verify that the DUT responds appropriately to those transactions.
- Avoid disturbing normal register or memory contents through the error transactions it injects.
- Coordinate with the environment’s assertion checking, outstanding-access tracking, reset state, and alert monitoring.
- Support operation with one or more RAL models / TL-UL interfaces.

---

## 2. General Behavioral Requirements

### 2.1 Error Transaction Generation

The module must generate TL-UL transactions that are expected to fail at the DUT. These transactions are used to exercise DUT error detection and response paths.

All generated TL-UL error transactions must:

- Be constrained so that the DUT is expected to return an error response.
- Not change CSR or memory contents.
- Be scheduled at a lower priority than normal register/memory accesses, so that concurrent normal traffic is not starved.
- Be randomized in address, data, timing, and other relevant attributes where applicable.
- Have a randomized request-abort / back-pressure likelihood.
- Complete within the environment’s transaction timeout; otherwise the module must report a fatal timeout error.

### 2.2 Outstanding-Access Accounting

The module must integrate with the environment’s outstanding-access accounting. When an error transaction is started, it must be recorded as outstanding. When it completes or times out, it must be removed from the outstanding set.

The main scenarios must wait until all outstanding injected accesses have completed before declaring the scenario finished.

### 2.3 Zero-Delay Mode

If the environment is configured for zero-delay operation, all generated error requests must be sent with zero request delay. Otherwise, randomized delays are allowed.

### 2.4 Reset Behavior

If the module observes that the DUT is under reset, it must:

- Stop generating new error transactions.
- Return from the current error scenario as promptly as possible.
- Not start new transactions while reset is active.

### 2.5 Assertion Management

Because the module intentionally generates illegal TL-UL traffic, it must disable TL-UL protocol assertions before beginning error injection. It must keep them disabled while injected traffic is outstanding, and re-enable them only after all outstanding injected transactions have completed.

This behavior must hold for all TL-UL interfaces being exercised, including when multiple interfaces are active.

---

## 3. TL-UL Error Scenarios

The module provides several distinct error-injection behaviors. Each behavior is run only when the target RAL model has the relevant feature.

### 3.1 Unmapped Address Access

If the target RAL model declares one or more unmapped address ranges, the module must:

- Randomly select one of the unmapped ranges.
- Generate an address within that range, constrained by the model’s valid address mask.
- Issue a TL-UL request to that address.
- Repeat the attempt a randomized number of times.

The generated access is intended to be rejected by the DUT because the address does not map to a valid device register or memory.

### 3.2 Write with Insufficient Byte Enables

For each register in the RAL model, in randomized order, the module must:

- Use the register’s own address.
- Generate a write request of type full-data or partial-data.
- Constrain the byte-enable mask so that not all bytes spanning the register’s active width are enabled.

In other words, the enabled byte lanes must be a strict subset of the byte lanes needed to write the full register. This request is expected to be rejected by the DUT and must not modify the register value.

### 3.3 TL-UL Protocol Error

The module must generate randomized TL-UL requests that intentionally violate the project’s TL-UL protocol rules, such as:

- Reserved or undefined opcodes.
- Invalid combinations of request size, address alignment, and byte-enable mask.
- Other protocol-level violations expected by the TL-UL device checkers.

These requests are not necessarily tied to a specific valid CSR or memory address. The scenario must repeat a randomized number of times.

### 3.4 Partial-Write Error to Memory Without Partial-Write Support

If the target RAL model has memory that does not support partial writes, the module must:

- Randomly select one such memory.
- Generate a write request to a word-aligned address within that memory.
- Make the request a partial write by using either a sub-word size or a byte-enable mask that leaves at least one byte lane inactive.

The memory is expected to reject the partial write. The memory contents must not be modified.

### 3.5 Read of Write-Only Memory

If the target RAL model has write-only memory, the module must:

- Randomly select one write-only memory.
- Generate a read request to an address within that memory.

The DUT must reject the read because the selected memory is write-only.

### 3.6 Write of Read-Only Memory

If the target RAL model has read-only memory, the module must:

- Randomly select one read-only memory.
- Generate a write request to an address within that memory.

The DUT must reject the write because the selected memory is read-only.

### 3.7 Combined TL-Error Scenario

The combined scenario must:

- Run for a caller-specified number of iterations.
- Launch one instance of the scenario for each active RAL model / TL-UL interface, with all interfaces exercised in parallel.
- For each iteration, create a randomized number of parallel error-injection threads.
- Each thread must randomly select one of the applicable error behaviors:
  - Protocol error.
  - Write with insufficient byte enables (only if CSRs exist).
  - Unmapped address access (only if unmapped addresses exist).
  - Partial-write error to memory (only if at least one memory rejects partial writes).
  - Read of write-only memory (only if write-only memory exists).
  - Write of read-only memory (only if read-only memory exists).
- A behavior must not be selected if the corresponding feature is not present.

If wait mode is enabled, the module must wait a randomized number of clock cycles between iterations. If reset is asserted during this wait, the module must abort the scenario as soon as possible.

---

## 4. TL-UL Integrity Error Scenario

### 4.1 Integrity Error Injection with Concurrent CSR Traffic

The integrity-error scenario must:

- Run for a caller-specified number of iterations.
- Launch one instance per active RAL model / TL-UL interface.
- For each interface, run a legal random CSR access stream concurrently with the integrity-error injection.
- Before injecting the integrity fault, read the integrity-error status fields and verify them against the RAL model.
- Randomly select a non-none integrity-error type.
- Randomize the access direction and data.
- Choose the access address either as a completely random address or, if the RAL model has memory, as an address within a randomly selected memory.
- Issue a TL-UL access with corrupted integrity protection fields or corrupted protected payload.

### 4.2 Serialization of Integrity Status Checks

When multiple TL-UL interfaces are active, the integrity-error status fields may be updated by one interface while another interface is checking them. The module must therefore ensure that only one interface at a time can be in the critical section that:

- Reads and verifies integrity-error status fields.
- Injects the integrity fault.
- Checks the DUT response.

This serialization prevents race conditions in status checking.

### 4.3 Excluding Status Fields from General CSR Checks

If more than one TL-UL interface is active, the module must exclude the integrity-error status fields from general CSR read/write checks. This prevents false failures caused by one interface updating those fields while another interface is checking them.

### 4.4 Integrity Error Response Checking

After an integrity-corrupted access is issued, the module must verify the DUT’s response:

- The configured integrity-error alert must be present in the list of alerts supported by the DUT. If it is not present, the module must report a fatal error.
- The fatal alert must be observed to trigger multiple times, confirming that the DUT keeps signaling the fatal alert until reset.
- The integrity-error status fields must be updated to the expected values.
- The module must predict the expected status values, then read and compare them.

### 4.5 Hard Initialization Between Iterations

After each iteration of the integrity-error scenario completes for all active interfaces, the module must return the DUT to a known state by performing a hard initialization. This clears the fatal alert state and prepares the DUT for the next iteration.

---

## 5. Pass-Through Memory Integrity Error Scenario

### 5.1 Scope

This scenario tests memories whose data-integrity information is passed through to the response rather than being fully checked or recomputed by the DUT. It is applicable only when such pass-through memories exist.

### 5.2 Identification of Pass-Through Memories

The module must identify memories in the RAL model that are configured for data-integrity pass-through.

If no such memories exist, no pass-through memory fault injection is performed. If normal CSR traffic is enabled, it may still run.

### 5.3 Baseline Read

For each pass-through memory, the module must:

- Randomly choose an offset within that memory.
- Compute the corresponding access address.
- Perform a read to that address.
- Verify that the read completes normally.
- Verify that the returned data integrity is valid.

This establishes that the memory and interface are functioning correctly before fault injection.

### 5.4 Fault Injection

The module must inject a data-integrity fault into the selected pass-through memory using a backdoor mechanism.

The concrete backdoor fault-injection behavior must be supplied by an IP-specific extension. If the extension is not implemented and the fault-injection hook is invoked, the module must report a fatal error.

### 5.5 Post-Injection Read

After injecting the fault, the module must:

- Read the same address again.
- Verify that the read completes normally at the transaction level.
- Verify that the returned data integrity is invalid.

During this test, the module must suppress any global data-integrity checking that would otherwise flag the intentionally corrupted data as a spontaneous error. The expected data-integrity failure is checked locally by this scenario.

### 5.6 Concurrent CSR Traffic

The pass-through memory scenario may run legal random CSR traffic concurrently with the fault-injection sequence if enabled by configuration.

### 5.7 Iteration and Initialization

The scenario must run for a caller-specified number of iterations. Each iteration must exercise all active RAL models / TL-UL interfaces. After each iteration, the module must perform a hard DUT initialization to restore a known state.

---

## 6. Summary of Key Behavioral Rules

- Error injection must target only invalid or rejected transactions; it must not modify CSR or memory values.
- Reset must cause prompt termination of active error generation.
- The module must manage TL-UL assertion state, leaving assertions re-enabled only after all injected traffic has drained.
- Integrity-error status checking must be race-free when multiple interfaces are active.
- Fatal alert and status-field behavior must be checked after integrity faults.
- Pass-through memory tests must verify valid data integrity before fault injection and invalid data integrity after fault injection.
- Hard initialization must be performed between integrity and pass-through memory test iterations to clear fatal alert state.
- The pass-through fault-injection hook must be implemented by an extension; absence of that implementation is a fatal condition.

# Behavioral Design Specification: RISC-V Core Wrapper (rv_core_ibex)

## 1. Purpose

This module wraps a 32-bit RISC-V CPU core and provides the interfaces needed to integrate it into a system using TileLink-UL buses. It exposes the core instruction and data memory ports as TL-UL host interfaces, provides a memory-mapped control/status interface, performs simple address translation, handles non-maskable interrupt events, generates random-number data from an entropy source, and reports error and alert conditions.

## 2. Functional Overview

The module must:

- Provide the behavior of a configurable RV32 RISC-V core, including the selected ISA extensions and microarchitectural options.
- Expose an instruction-side TL-UL host interface.
- Expose a data-side TL-UL host interface.
- Expose a TL-UL device interface for control and status registers.
- Perform programmable address translation independently for instruction and data accesses.
- Provide non-maskable interrupt (NMI) functionality for escalation and watchdog events.
- Provide a polling-style random data register filled from the entropy distribution network.
- Record recoverable and fatal error events.
- Generate alert handshake outputs for software-visible and hardware-detected alert conditions.
- Provide reset, power, debug, crash-dump, scan, and memory-configuration behavior needed by the core.

## 3. Reset and Clock Behavior

The module must operate from a main clock and an active-low asynchronous reset for the core and its main interfaces.

The module must also support separate clock domains for the entropy request/response interface and for the escalation receiver interface. Events arriving in these domains must be safely handled and made available in the main clock domain.

The module must provide a reset feedback output that indicates the state of the main reset. This output must be asserted while the main reset is asserted and deasserted when the main reset is released.

During reset:

- The core must not fetch or execute instructions.
- The module must not initiate new TL-UL transactions.
- Random data must be invalid.
- Status and sticky error bits must be at their reset values.

## 4. CPU Core Behavior

The core must operate as a RISC-V RV32 processor with the configured features. The following configuration classes must affect behavior as selected:

- Base ISA: RV32I, optionally RV32E.
- Multiplication/division extension: none, single-cycle, or multi-cycle.
- Bit-manipulation extension: none or enabled.
- Physical memory protection: enable, granularity, and number of regions.
- Register-file implementation.
- Pipeline options such as branch-target ALU and writeback stage.
- Instruction cache enable and ECC behavior.
- Branch prediction enable.
- Debug-trigger enable.
- Secure core mode and associated random constants.
- Debug-module halt and exception addresses.

The module must use the supplied hart identifier for the core’s hart ID. The core must begin fetching after reset from the supplied boot address.

The module must accept debug request input and pass it to the core so the core can enter debug mode according to its debug behavior.

The module must apply the supplied memory configuration to the core’s embedded memories.

The core must only be allowed to fetch instructions when both the life-cycle enable and the power-manager enable are active. If either enable is inactive, the core must remain in a non-fetching state and must retain its architectural state. Fetching must resume when both enables are active again.

The module must output core sleep status so that external power management can observe whether the core is sleeping.

The module must output crash-dump information reflecting the core’s crash state when the core produces such information.

## 5. Instruction and Data TL-UL Interfaces

### 5.1 General Bus Requirements

The instruction and data ports must behave as TL-UL hosts compliant with the TileLink-UL specification and the project’s TL-UL user-extension conventions.

All transactions are limited to single-beat requests; no burst support is required.

The module must drive the TL-UL user attributes so that downstream logic can distinguish instruction transactions from data transactions and can validate command/data integrity.

The module must support backpressure on both request and response channels according to TL-UL protocol.

### 5.2 Instruction Interface

The instruction interface must carry instruction-fetch requests only. It must not issue write transactions.

Instruction fetches must be presented as TL-UL read transactions. The module must set the instruction-type attribute for these transactions.

If the core is configured with an instruction cache, the instruction interface must support a larger number of outstanding requests than when no cache is configured.

The instruction interface must pass back to the core:

- Fetched instruction data.
- Instruction fetch error indications.
- Instruction bus integrity error indications.

### 5.3 Data Interface

The data interface must carry all load and store traffic from the core.

It must support:

- Word, halfword, and byte reads.
- Word, halfword, and byte writes.
- Byte-lane strobes for partial writes.

The module must present data accesses as TL-UL read or write transactions with the appropriate opcode, size, and byte-mask attributes.

The data interface must pass back to the core:

- Load data.
- Store/load error indications.
- Data bus integrity error indications.

### 5.4 Bus Pipelining and Outstanding Transactions

The module must support a configurable pipelining mode.

When pipelining is disabled:

- The instruction and data interfaces must operate with minimal added latency.
- A request or response may pass through the module without an extra internal pipeline cycle.

When pipelining is enabled:

- The instruction and data interfaces must buffer requests and responses.
- At least one cycle of latency must be added.
- The number of outstanding transactions must be sufficient for the configured core/cache behavior.

### 5.5 Bus Error and Integrity Behavior

If a TL-UL response has `d_error` asserted, the module must report the error to the core for the corresponding instruction fetch or data access.

If a TL-UL response has an integrity error, the module must:

- Report an error to the core for the affected access.
- Record the event as a fatal integrity error.
- Cause the corresponding fatal hardware alert to be generated.

The module must preserve valid TL-UL integrity attributes on outgoing transactions.

In secure core mode, the core supplies the appropriate integrity values and the module must pass them through.

In non-secure core mode, the module itself must generate correct integrity values for outgoing TL-UL commands and write data.

## 6. Simple Address Translation

The module must provide separate address translation for the instruction interface and the data interface.

Each translation function must support two programmable regions per interface.

Each region must be enabled or disabled independently.

For each enabled region, the module must compare the incoming address against a naturally aligned power-of-two matching range. The matching range is programmed using a NAPOT-style encoding.

When an address matches an enabled region:

- The address must be replaced by the corresponding remap address.
- The low offset within the matching region must be preserved in the translated address.

When an address matches no enabled region:

- The address must pass through unchanged.

When an address matches multiple enabled regions:

- The lowest-indexed region must take priority.

Instruction address translation and data address translation must be independent. Changing a translation configuration must affect subsequent accesses after the configuration update has been completed.

## 7. Control and Status Interface

The module must provide a memory-mapped TL-UL device interface for software access to control and status registers.

The interface must:

- Support reads and writes to implemented registers.
- Return a TL-UL error response for accesses to unimplemented or invalid addresses.
- Reject writes that violate protocol or integrity rules; a rejected write must not modify register state.

The control/status register space must provide at least the following functionality:

- Instruction address-translation region controls.
- Data address-translation region controls.
- NMI status and enable controls.
- Random-data status and data registers.
- Error status sticky bits.
- Alert test controls and software-triggered alert controls.

Status bits updated by hardware must be cleared by software using the appropriate write semantics.

## 8. NMI, Escalation, and Watchdog Behavior

### 8.1 Escalation Input

The module must receive escalation signaling and respond according to the escalation protocol.

When the escalation receiver detects an active escalation request, the module must set a sticky alert-NMI status bit in the main clock domain.

The escalation signaling and the main core logic may be in different clock or reset domains. The module must ensure that an escalation event is correctly transferred into the main clock domain before it affects core-visible NMI state.

### 8.2 Watchdog Input

When the watchdog NMI bark input is asserted, the module must set a sticky watchdog-NMI status bit.

The watchdog input must be synchronized into the main clock domain before affecting core-visible NMI state.

### 8.3 NMI Generation

The module must combine the sticky alert-NMI and watchdog-NMI status bits with the corresponding NMI enable bits.

If any enabled NMI status bit is set, the module must present an NMI request to the core.

The sticky status bits must remain set after the initiating input deasserts. Software must clear them explicitly.

If software clears one NMI status bit while another NMI status bit remains enabled and set, the NMI must remain asserted to the core.

### 8.4 Regular Interrupts

The module must pass the standard software, timer, and external interrupt inputs through to the core as regular interrupt requests.

## 9. Random Number Generation

The module must provide a 32-bit random data register filled from the entropy distribution network.

The module must also provide a random-data-valid status bit and a FIPS status bit.

After reset:

- Random data must be invalid.
- The module must request new random data from the entropy interface.
- The request must remain pending until an entropy response is received.

When a valid entropy response arrives:

- The 32-bit data must be stored.
- The random-data-valid status must be set.
- The FIPS status must be updated from the response.

When software reads the random-data register while valid data is present:

- The stored data must be invalidated.
- The random-data-valid status must be cleared.
- A new request for random data must be made.

It must never be possible for the module to have no valid random data and no pending entropy request.

If software reads the random-data register while no valid data is present, the module must continue to maintain a pending request and must load a future entropy response when it arrives.

## 10. Error Recording and Alert Generation

### 10.1 Error Status Recording

The module must record the following error categories in sticky status bits:

- Configuration-interface integrity error.
- Instruction or data bus integrity error.
- Fatal core error.
- Recoverable core error.

When any of these events occurs, the corresponding status bit must be set. If the same event occurs while the bit is already set, the bit must remain set.

Software must be able to clear these sticky status bits through the control/status interface.

### 10.2 Alert Outputs

The module must generate the following alert classes:

- Fatal software alert.
- Recoverable software alert.
- Fatal hardware alert.
- Recoverable hardware alert.

The fatal hardware alert must be generated when any of the following occurs:

- A configuration-interface integrity error.
- An instruction or data bus integrity error.
- A fatal core error.

The recoverable hardware alert must be generated when a recoverable core error occurs.

Software-induced alert controls must allow software to trigger fatal and recoverable software alerts directly.

The recoverable software alert trigger must be cleared when the alert is acknowledged.

### 10.3 Alert Test

The module must provide a test mechanism for each alert class.

When software writes the test control for an alert, the module must transmit a test alert on the corresponding alert interface.

A test alert must not set error status bits.

### 10.4 Alert Handshake

All alert outputs must follow the project alert handshake protocol.

The asynchronous behavior of alert handshakes must be configurable per alert.

## 11. DFT / Scan Behavior

The module must support scan test mode.

When scan mode indicates test mode, the core test-enable behavior must be activated.

When scan mode is inactive, the functional test enable must be inactive.

The module must accept a scan reset input and make it available to the core for scan-chain reset behavior.

## 12. Interface Summary

The module must provide the following interface roles:

- Main clock and reset.
- Separate clock/reset for entropy distribution network.
- Separate clock/reset for escalation receiver.
- Reset feedback output.
- Instruction TL-UL host.
- Data TL-UL host.
- Configuration TL-UL device.
- Standard RISC-V interrupt inputs.
- Escalation request/response interface.
- Watchdog NMI input.
- Debug request input.
- Crash-dump output.
- Life-cycle and power-manager enable inputs.
- Core sleep output.
- Entropy request/response interface.
- Alert receiver/transmitter interfaces.
- Memory configuration input.
- Hart ID and boot-address inputs.
- Scan reset and scan-mode inputs.

All external interfaces must behave according to their respective protocol specifications and must be used only as described in this specification.

# Specification: TL-UL Request Integrity Checker

## Overview

This module is a passive integrity checker for TileLink Uncached Light (TL-UL) requests. It observes a host-to-device request presented on a TL-UL interface and validates the integrity sideband information associated with that request.

The request carries two integrity codes:

- a **command integrity code**, which protects the request’s command attributes, such as operation type, address, size, mask, source identifier, and related control information.
- a **data integrity code**, which protects the data payload carried with the request.

The module produces a single error indication when either integrity check fails.

## Functional Requirements

### No Request Present

When no request is being presented on the TL-UL interface, the error indication must be deasserted.

### Valid Request with Correct Integrity

When a request is presented and both integrity codes match the values expected for the protected command and data fields, the error indication must be deasserted.

### Command Integrity Failure

When a request is presented and the received command integrity code does not match the value expected for the protected command attributes, the error indication must be asserted.

This includes failures caused by:

- corruption of the command integrity code itself,
- corruption of one or more protected command attributes,
- any other condition that makes the command integrity code inconsistent with the command fields it protects.

### Data Integrity Failure

When a request is presented and the received data integrity code does not match the data payload carried with the request, the error indication must be asserted.

The data integrity check applies to every presented request, regardless of whether the request is a read or a write. For a read request, the data field is still checked against the integrity code carried with that request.

### Combined Failure

If both the command integrity check and the data integrity check fail at the same time, the error indication must be asserted.

The module provides only a single combined error indication. It does not report which of the two integrity checks failed.

### Error Indication is Not Latched

The error indication is transactional and not stored. It is asserted only while a request is being presented and one or both integrity checks fail. When the request is withdrawn or the request-valid condition is removed, the error indication returns to deasserted.

### Scope of Checking

The module validates only integrity consistency. It does not:

- validate TileLink protocol opcode legality,
- check address decoding or access permissions,
- detect unsupported size or mask combinations,
- inspect response-channel integrity,
- modify, block, or respond to the request.

A request with an unusual or unsupported TileLink encoding is not considered an integrity failure as long as its integrity codes are consistent with the command fields and data actually carried by that request.
